title: Come to learn to live
hook: Attalus: some come to lectures to learn talk, not life (Letters 108)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the willing are led, Cleanthes' line in Seneca's Latin. Your line was led, not dragged. Did you take the first step toward something hard before the complaining was done? Day four hundred eighty-four.
screen: `THE WILLING ARE LED — LED, NOT DRAGGED.`

segments.voice: Picture a podcast you've listened to for years. You could quote it. You've sent episodes to friends. Now the uncomfortable question: has anything in your actual week changed because of it? Letter 108 is an old man remembering being young and hungry for exactly that kind of listening. Seneca says that as a student he was always first into the lecture hall of a Stoic teacher named Attalus, and the last to leave. Even on Attalus' walks, he'd trail along asking questions. And Attalus, it turns out, had a warning for students like him. Today: come to learn to live.
screen: `THE PODCAST YOU COULD QUOTE.` → `FIRST IN, LAST OUT.` → `ATTALUS HAD A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First, Attalus' rule. Whoever goes to a philosopher, he used to say, should carry home something good every day, and go home either healthier or at least easier to heal. Not more impressive. Healthier. Second, the audience who came for the show. Seneca describes people who treat the lecture hall like a theater: they come for the pleasure of hearing, they cheer the clever phrases, and they take notes on the words, not on the life. Some even nod along to a line about poverty and then go home and live exactly as before. Third, one line read two ways. Seneca uses a verse from Virgil, the poet, saying that the best days of our lives are the first to slip away. A scholar of grammar, he says, will notice how Virgil likes to pair illness with old age, and make a note. The philosopher hears something else: the best days are going, so begin now. Same line, two readers. One collects it. One is changed by it. Fourth, his sharp summary. Seneca complains that among teachers and students alike, what used to be philosophy has turned into philology: the love of wisdom became the love of words. In Latin: quae philosophia fuit, facta philologia est. He isn't against learning words. He's against stopping there. Which is why this path ends every day with a carry. The carry is Attalus' rule in miniature: one small good thing, taken home.
screen: `TAKE SOMETHING GOOD HOME EVERY DAY.` · `THE AUDIENCE WHO CAME FOR THE SHOW.` · `ONE VIRGIL LINE, TWO READERS.` · `PHILOSOPHY BECAME PHILOLOGY.` · then, large: `LEARN TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Think back over this path, or anything you've read or heard lately. Pick one lesson you liked but haven't used. Just one. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence. Now shrink it into a single action you could do in the next few hours: a text you could send, a reply you could soften, ten minutes you could protect. Picture yourself doing it, where, and when. That's the difference between collecting a line and taking it home. The bell holds the time.
Come to learn to live. Attalus' warning, through Seneca: go to a teacher to come home healthier, not just better at talking. Today's word.
screen: `COME TO LEARN TO LIVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: learn to live. Do the one action you just chose before the day is out. Tonight, ask yourself Attalus' question: what good did I carry home? Day four hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Many people who study Stoic writing keep a short daily note of one idea they actually used that day, following the old teachers' rule that learning should change how you live.

original.note: Latin from Greek, Letters 108: love of wisdom turned into love of words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good student remembers everything.
what it means: Attalus' test was whether you went home healthier, not cleverer.
what a scholar hears: 'philologia' for Seneca means fussing over words and texts, the opposite of the practical philosophy he wants; the Virgil line comes from the Georgics, Book 3.

notes: Latin of Letters 108.23 quoted in the original; confirm exact wording and section.
Attalus' rule (take home some good daily, go home sounder or more curable) and Seneca being first to arrive and last to leave, and walking with him: Letters 108.3–4; confirm.
The Virgil line (optima quaeque dies...) and the grammarian's note on 'morbi' and 'senectus': Letters 108.24–29, Georgics 3.66–68; confirm the details.
The comment about the carry as Attalus' rule in miniature is the path's own framing, not Seneca's.
